1. Structural and Motility Disorders

Congenital defects

  • Esophageal atresia = disconnected lumen (proximal esophagus cut off from the distal esophagus; swallowed material cannot pass). Agenesis = no esophagus at all. Stenosis = incomplete atresia, a narrowing; congenital or acquired (inflammatory scarring, surgery).
  • Tracheoesophageal fistula = abnormal luminal connection between the esophagus and trachea → aspiration into the lungs → suffocation or pneumonia.
  • Atresia and fistula can occur separately or together in varying combinations.
Congenital defects (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Diverticula

Outpouching of all three layers of the esophageal wall (seen on barium swallow as a pouch that traps contrast).

TypeLocationFeatures
ZenkerProximal esophagusMost common; elderly; asymptomatic or accumulates food → regurgitation, halitosis
Midesophageal (traction)Mid esophagus, near the tracheal bifurcationUncommon; tuberculosis or other inflammatory scarring
EpiphrenicDistal esophagus, just above the lower esophageal sphincter (LES)Rare; associated with hiatal hernia
Zenker diverticulum (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Hiatal hernia

Protrusion of part of the stomach into the thoracic cavity through the esophageal hiatus.

TypeFeatures
Sliding (95%)Stomach slides up through the hiatus; associated with GERD
ParaesophagealLarger segment of stomach pinches up through the hiatus; prone to strangulation; often needs surgery
Hiatal hernia (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Esophageal webs and Schatzki rings

Mucosal protrusions into the lumen causing partial obstruction.

WebsRings (Schatzki)
LocationUpper esophagusLower esophagus
ShapeSemicircumferential (wedge-like)Circumferential
AssociationPlummer-Vinson syndrome: iron-deficiency anemia + esophageal webs + dysphagia; middle-aged females. Also GERD, graft-versus-host diseaseHiatal hernia (A ring and B ring just above the hernia)
Webs and rings (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Achalasia

Motility disorder with (1) incomplete LES relaxation and increased LES tone and (2) diminished peristalsis; the sphincter stays tight and material cannot pass.

  • Primary: idiopathic degeneration of myenteric ganglion cells. Normally excitatory and inhibitory neurons balance contraction and relaxation; here the inhibitory neurons are lost (immune attack), leaving unopposed excitatory tone → constant constriction.
  • Secondary: Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi destroys myenteric neurons along the GI tract); restrictive disease that narrows the junction (malignancy, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis).
  • Clinical: progressive dysphagia and nocturnal regurgitation. Barium swallow: bird-beak (rat-tail) with a massively dilated esophagus above the narrowed junction. Minor increased risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Treatment: botulinum toxin injection relieves symptoms temporarily; surgery is curative.
Achalasia (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Achalasia clinical (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

2. Esophageal Injury and Varices

Mallory-Weiss tears and Boerhaave syndrome

Mallory-Weiss tearBoerhaave syndrome
InjuryLongitudinal lacerations of the mucosa near the gastroesophageal junctionTransmural tear and rupture
CauseSevere retching or vomiting, most often with alcohol intoxicationProlonged, severe retching
CourseMost often self-limited; can cause GI bleeding: painful hematemesisLeakage of esophageal contents into the mediastinum; medical emergency, high mortality
Mallory-Weiss tears (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Esophageal varices

  • Dilated, tortuous submucosal veins in the lower esophagus (and proximal stomach).
  • Pathogenesis: impaired blood flow through the liver/portal tract → portal hypertension → collateral channels form between the liver vasculature and the lower esophagus/upper stomach → pressure stays high → congestion and dilation of esophageal veins.
  • Most often from liver cirrhosis; other vascular obstruction to the liver can also cause them. Diagnosed by endoscopy.
  • Complications: GI bleeding with painless hematemesis; rupture and hemorrhage is a medical emergency (band ligation, sclerotherapy, balloon tamponade).
Esophageal varices (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

3. Esophagitis

Inflammation of the esophagus. Causes: chemical, infectious (especially in immunocompromised patients), eosinophilic, and reflux.

Chemical esophagitis

  • Acute inflammation with dysphagia and odynophagia (painful swallowing). Causes: irritants (alcohol, hot drinks, smoking), pill-induced (a pill lodges and dissolves, concentrated local damage), radiation.
  • Mucosal/submucosal neutrophil infiltration; no features distinguish the different chemical causes.
Chemical esophagitis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Infectious esophagitis

OrganismGrossMicroscopic
HSVPunched-out ulcers (round, red, like a hole punch)Infection limited to the ulcer edge: multinucleated, ground-glass squamous cells; Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions; IHC for HSV can help
CMVLinear, well-demarcated ulcer, may be covered in exudateEnlarged cells with nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions (granular appearance)
CandidaPseudomembranous plaques (like oral thrush)GMS (Gomori methenamine silver) stain: fungi black on a blue background
Infectious esophagitis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE)

  • Chronic, immune-mediated disorder associated with atopy (genetic predisposition to allergy). Presents with dysphagia, food impaction, regurgitation (depending on age of onset).
  • Pathogenesis: allergen exposure → Th2 response → eosinophils recruited to the epithelium → activation of mast cells and basophils → immune-mediated epithelial damage and barrier dysfunction → tissue remodeling and fibrosis.
  • Morphology: superficial intraepithelial eosinophils (most characteristic), basal zone hyperplasia, lamina propria fibrosis. Endoscopy: feline (ring-like) esophagus from remodeling. Findings are characteristic but not specific (also seen in GERD).
Eosinophilic esophagitis pathogenesis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Eosinophilic esophagitis morphology (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Reflux esophagitis (GERD)

  • The most common cause of esophagitis: inflammation from reflux of gastric contents into the distal esophagus; the disease is gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Abnormal relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter lets acid back up; presents as heartburn.
  • Causes: gastric distention (increased volume or delayed emptying); change in intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, straining; long term: hiatal hernia, pregnancy); alcohol and tobacco.
  • Complications: erosion/ulceration; stricture (chronic fibrosis after repeated damage and healing); Barrett esophagus → adenocarcinoma.
  • Morphology: grossly unremarkable early (erosions/ulcers in advanced disease). Microscopic: eosinophils in the mucosa (fewer and less superficial than EoE), elongated lamina propria papillae, basal zone hyperplasia. Characteristic but not exclusive.
Reflux esophagitis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Reflux esophagitis histology (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Comparison: eosinophilic vs reflux esophagitis

EosinophilicReflux
CausesAtopy, exposure to allergens → immune-mediated damageLower esophageal sphincter relaxation, gastric distention, intra-abdominal pressure change, tobacco, alcohol
MorphologySuperficial intraepithelial eosinophils, basal zone hyperplasia, “feline” endoscopyIntraepithelial eosinophils, basal zone hyperplasia, lamina propria papillae extension
ComplicationsDysphagia, regurgitation, food impaction, no link to Barrett esophagusErosion, strictures, Barrett esophagus
Why similar morphology?Both cause chronic epithelial injury and repair, so injury/repair changes (basal zone hyperplasia, immune infiltrates, fibrosis) appear in both.

4. Barrett Esophagus

  • Intestinal metaplasia of the distal esophagus from chronic GERD: normal (fragile) stratified squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar glandular epithelium with goblet cells, which resists acid better (an adaptation to chronic injury).
  • Starts at the gastroesophageal junction and pushes the Z line (squamocolumnar junction) upward. Can regress if GERD is managed; continued injury → progressive dysplasia → adenocarcinoma.
  • Endoscopy: pale squamous mucosa vs salmon-colored, velvety intestinal mucosa; abnormal Z line with tongue-like protrusions of intestinal mucosa.
Barrett esophagus (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Barrett esophagus histology (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Dysplastic progression

StageFeatures
Metaplasia (no dysplasia)Wrong tissue for the site but normal surface maturation, normal nuclear polarity, normal architecture
Low-grade dysplasiaHyperchromasia, hyperplasia, atypia with increased N:C ratio, little or no surface maturation; architecture still near normal
High-grade dysplasiaSame as low grade plus architectural distortion: crypt budding/branching and overcrowded glands
Barrett dysplasia (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

5. Esophageal Neoplasia

Adenocarcinoma

  • Malignant neoplasm of the distal esophagus (often at the gastroesophageal junction), arising from chronic GERD and Barrett esophagus.
  • Epidemiology: males (7x) and Caucasian ancestry. Much less common than SCC globally, but US incidence is rising: 5% of esophageal cancers (1970) → 60% today.
  • Risk factors: Barrett esophagus, tobacco and obesity, but not alcohol.
  • Pathogenesis: the same prolonged mucosal damage that causes Barrett esophagus accumulates mutations: TP53 and CDKN2A loss → chromosomal instability; later epigenetic silencing of tumor suppressors and oncogene amplification.
  • Micro: invasive glandular structures scattered in the surrounding tissue (it arises from glandular metaplastic epithelium).
Adenocarcinoma (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
The whole storyLES relaxation → acid reflux → repeated damage → metaplasia to hardy intestinal-type cells (Barrett) → more mutations in tumor suppressors/oncogenes → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma. A hiatal hernia can start this by weakening the LES.
GERD to adenocarcinoma (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)

  • Malignant neoplasm of squamous epithelium, most often in the middle esophagus (also proximal or distal); ulcerated, exophytic mass.
  • Most common esophageal cancer globally. Males, more common in African American ancestry.
  • Risk factors: tobacco and alcohol (major); irradiation, achalasia, diet (very hot tea), caustic injury.
  • Pathogenesis: chronic epithelial injury → dysplasia → invasive neoplasia; TP53 mutation common.
  • Micro: nests of squamous cells invading muscle, keratin pearls, intercellular bridges (no glands).
Squamous cell carcinoma (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Squamous cell carcinoma histology (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Clinical (both tumors)

  • Progressive dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss; CT shows luminal narrowing.
  • Lymph node metastasis is common by the time symptoms arise. 5-year survival <20% overall; ~75–80% if localized.
Esophageal carcinoma clinical (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Comparison

AdenocarcinomaSCC
Causes / risk factorsGERD → Barrett esophagus, tobacco, obesityExposure to carcinogens (tobacco, alcohol, achalasia, very hot tea, etc.)
Tumor siteDistal esophagus / gastroesophageal junctionAnywhere (most common in the middle)
MicroscopicGlandular morphologyNests of squamous cells, keratin pearls, intercellular bridges

6. Study Guide Key: Guiding Questions and Morphology-Mechanism Table

Guiding questions (from the study guide)

Atresia vs tracheoesophageal fistula in a newborn?Atresia: upper and lower esophagus disconnected → feeding intolerance, regurgitation, aspiration. Fistula: abnormal trachea-esophagus connection → aspiration and choking.
Relationship between GERD and hiatal hernia?A hiatal hernia weakens the anti-reflux mechanisms and predisposes to GERD; chronic GERD can further compromise esophageal function and LES competency, creating a cycle.
One primary and one secondary cause of achalasia?Primary: idiopathic loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons (failed LES relaxation, aperistalsis). Secondary: Chagas disease (destroys ganglia) or malignancy near the LES.
Mallory-Weiss vs Boerhaave?Same: retching/vomiting injury; bleeding. Different: Mallory-Weiss is mucosal and often self-limited (hematemesis); Boerhaave is transmural, causes mediastinitis, and is a severe emergency.
How does cirrhosis lead to esophageal hemorrhage?Cirrhosis raises resistance to portal flow → portal hypertension → collaterals to the lower esophagus/upper stomach → dilated submucosal veins (varices) → rupture → massive upper GI bleeding.
Distinguishing infectious esophagitis?HSV: punched-out superficial ulcers, infection at the ulcer edge, multinucleated cells with inclusions. CMV: linear well-demarcated ulcer, enlarged cells with nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions. Candida: pseudomembranous plaques, GMS-positive.
EoE vs reflux esophagitis pathogenesis, and why similar morphology?EoE: allergy-driven Th2 immune injury. Reflux: repeated acid injury. Both cause chronic injury and repair, so basal zone hyperplasia, immune infiltrates and fibrosis appear in both.
Why do squamous cells become columnar (not another type) in Barrett?Columnar epithelium resists chronic acid and bile better than stratified squamous epithelium; chronic injury reprograms stem cells toward an intestinal-type columnar phenotype adapted to the reflux environment.
Barrett vs normal esophageal mucosa?Barrett: intestinal metaplasia, columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Normal: stratified squamous epithelium without goblet cells.
How does a hiatal hernia progress to adenocarcinoma?Hernia weakens the LES → GERD → chronic injury and Barrett esophagus → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma.
Why are Barrett-associated tumors glandular?Barrett replaces squamous epithelium with gland-forming columnar epithelium, so malignant transformation produces adenocarcinoma.
Causes of esophageal SCC vs adenocarcinoma?SCC: tobacco, alcohol, irradiation, achalasia, diet, caustic injury. Adenocarcinoma: also tobacco and irradiation, not strongly alcohol; strongly linked to obesity and chronic GERD/Barrett.
Why are esophageal cancers caught late?Early lesions are asymptomatic and later symptoms (dysphagia) resemble benign disease; by the time symptoms arise, metastasis has likely occurred.

Morphology-mechanism table (click to reveal)

For each image: name the pathology, the pathophysiology, and why dysphagia occurs.

Image: answerZenker diverticulum (outpouching in the proximal esophagus). Increased luminal pressure herniates mucosa/submucosa through a weak region. Dysphagia: the outpouching narrows the lumen and traps material, narrowing it further.
Image: answerAchalasia (dilated proximal esophagus, narrowed distal esophagus). Failure of LES relaxation and aperistalsis from destruction of inhibitory neurons. Dysphagia: functional obstruction; the LES stays stiff and peristalsis fails.
Image: answerSchatzki ring (circumferential narrowing toward the distal esophagus). Localized mucosal narrowing associated with hiatal hernia, possibly fibrosis after GERD injury. Dysphagia: physically restricts passage.
Images: answerSquamous cell carcinoma (endoscopy lesion; histology with keratinization). Carcinogens (tobacco, alcohol) cause mutagenesis and malignant transformation. Dysphagia: the growing tumor obstructs the lumen.
Images: answerEosinophilic esophagitis (concentric “feline” rings; superficial eosinophils, basal zone hyperplasia, no atypia). Allergen exposure drives an immune response in the epithelium. Dysphagia: chronic inflammation causes fibrosis and remodeling, forming strictures that narrow the lumen.
Images: answerAdenocarcinoma (distal lesion with Barrett esophagus around it; dysplastic glands). Mostly GERD → intestinal metaplasia → Barrett → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma (also tobacco, obesity). Dysphagia: the growing tumor obstructs the lumen.
